title: Chaitanya's singing streets
hookLine: a man in Bengal leads the whole town singing through the streets, and it becomes a method
carry: singing God's name is itself devotion
tomorrow: who is the one asking 'who am I?'
last: MOTHER, I DIDN'T EAT THE BUTTER.

cards: Maybe you've heard it at a temple, a yoga studio, or on a city sidewalk. One voice sings a line. Everyone sings it back.

Drums, little hand cymbals, sometimes a harmonium wheezing along. The same few names, over and over, a little faster each time, until people who walked in stiff and shy are swaying, eyes closed, some of them crying.
It can look like a concert. It's older than that, and it's meant as a method. Today: kirtan.

teach.b: Kirtan comes from the Sanskrit kirt: to mention, to tell, to praise aloud. It's the second of the nine forms of devotion. The Alvars and Nayanars sang.
But in Bengal, Chaitanya of Nabadwip turned singing into a movement. He'd lead crowds through the streets, singing the names of Krishna, dancing, arms raised.
Tradition says that when the local authorities tried to ban the public singing, he answered with an even bigger procession.
For Chaitanya's followers, the Gaudiya Vaishnavas, singing the divine name isn't a warm-up for devotion. It is the devotion. God, they say, is present in the name.
Why does it work as a method?
It's call and response, so you don't have to know anything; you just repeat. It uses the body: breath, voice, rhythm. It's done together, so the group carries your shyness.
And it runs on repetition, which, people who sing it say, slowly quiets the part of the mind that keeps commentating. That's this whole week. The nine doors, one room.
Andal's garland and the singer on the priest's shoulders. Kannappa's eye. Mira's cup of poison.

teach.h: SINGING GOD'S NAME IS ITSELF DEVOTION.
teach.b: And now a whole street singing. Bhakti says the road to God can be love, all the way. Tomorrow, the third path, which asks a very different question.

how: Kirtan is sung in temples, homes and public processions across the Hindu world: a leader sings a line of divine names and the group answers, usually with drums (mridanga), small cymbals (kartal) and harmonium; Gaudiya Vaishnavas, including ISKCON, make chanting the name central to daily practice.

a concert of sacred music, put on for an audience

it's far older; Chaitanya led street kirtan in Bengal long before any yoga studio.
the word kirtan comes from a root meaning to praise or tell aloud
kirt: to mention, to tell, to praise.
in kirtan, you need to know the songs before joining
it's call and response: one voice sings, everyone repeats.

games.q: you're Chaitanya. the local authorities have banned public singing of God's names. what does tradition say you do?
o: sing quietly indoors from now on.
games.why: tradition says he organized a larger singing procession, and the ban was dropped.

practice: Pick one short name or word that means something to you: if you pray, a name of God, like Rama, Krishna, Shiva or Om; if not, a word like peace, or a loved one's name.
Say it softly on the out-breath, then hear it in your head as if a room answered back. Let it get slower, not faster, and let the commentary quiet.

wordCard.voice: Bhakti yoga, part seven: kirtan, singing the divine name together, call and response. For Chaitanya's followers, the name itself is the devotion.

orig.note: Sanskrit: kirtana, praising aloud; from kirt, to mention, tell, praise.

carryVoice: Your line: singing God's name is itself devotion. Seven days of love as the road, ending with a whole street singing. See you on the next path.
